chicken-thigh-baked-or-broiled-skin-not-.title: Chicken thigh, baked or broiled, skin not eaten, from pre‑cooked (831)

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh is meat from the thigh portion of a chicken, pre‑cooked (code 831) and ready for further baking or broiling. It is high in protein, low in fat thanks to the removed skin, and suitable for a wide range of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thigh meat contains more iron than breast meat because of its denser muscle fibers.
When baked without skin, the meat stays juicy while excess fat drips away, making the dish less caloric.
Chicken thighs are a staple in many world cuisines, from French coq au vin to Asian teriyaki.
Pre‑cooked pieces (code 831) reduce cooking time and ensure even heat distribution.
Thigh meat has a richer flavor than breast, popular among those who prefer a more robust taste.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Skinless thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin dramatically cuts saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chicken thigh provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Selenium present in the meat contributes to antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow bacteria such as Salmonella or Campylobacter to grow.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in processed product
items.content: Pre‑cooked pieces may contain added salt; people limiting sodium should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh can be baked at 180‑200 °C for 20‑30 minutes, pan‑seared 5‑7 minutes per side, or cooked in a slow cooker. Season with herbs, spices, and a drizzle of olive oil before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at +2‑+4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at ‑18 °C for 2‑3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.

lamb-or-mutton-rice-and-vegetables-exclu.title: Lamb or Mutton with Rice and Vegetables in Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb (or mutton) is the meat of sheep, known for its rich flavor and tender texture. Combined with fluffy rice and a mix of vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens), the dish offers a balanced taste, while the gravy adds moisture and depth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is a great source of heme iron, which is highly bioavailable.
Around the world lamb is prepared as kebabs, stews, and pilafs.
Rice is one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 5,000 years.
Vegetables such as zucchini, bell pepper, and cauliflower are often added for color and texture.
A broth‑based gravy enhances the absorption of nutrients from the meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lamb provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in lamb is easily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the meat and rice supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice delivers slowly digestible carbs, promoting stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants
items.content: The added vegetables contribute dietary fiber and antioxidants that benefit digestive health.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Lamb can contain notable amounts of saturated fat; individuals with heart disease should moderate portions.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to lamb proteins.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should use it sparingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lamb can be roasted, braised, or pan‑seared, then mixed with boiled rice and sautéed vegetables. Pour the gravy over the dish at the end of cooking for extra juiciness. Serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw lamb refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days or freeze at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Cooked leftovers should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp are crustaceans from the families Penaeidae and Crangonidae. When steamed or boiled, they retain a delicate flavor and tender texture. Shrimp are commonly used in salads, soups, pastas, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp can change color depending on their environment and stress level.
They are capable of regenerating lost limbs.
More than 7 million tons of shrimp are produced worldwide each year.
Shrimp are a major source of protein in many coastal countries.
The largest shrimp, the giant tiger shrimp, can reach up to 30 cm in length.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, shrimp contain very little fat, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Shrimp supply zinc, iron, and phosphorus, which are involved in numerous metabolic processes.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Shrimp farmed in polluted waters can accumulate mercury and cadmium.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed or boiled shrimp can be served as a snack, added to salads, rice and noodle dishes, soups, and used in sushi and rolls. Before cooking they are usually peeled and deveined.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh shrimp in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for no more than 2 days. Frozen shrimp should be kept at –18 °C and used within 6‑12 months. Thaw frozen shrimp in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced green tea in a bottle is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage made from green tea leaves that are brewed, filtered, and chilled without any added sugar. It retains the light, vegetal flavor of green tea with a gentle bitterness and a crisp, cooling finish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is rich in polyphenols, especially epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), known for strong antioxidant activity.
Bottled iced tea is often packaged in clear glass or PET bottles to showcase its clear, bright color.
Being unsweetened, the drink is very low in calories—about 0–5 kcal per 100 ml.
Traditional green tea cultivation originates in China, Japan, and parts of India.
Cooling the tea can accentuate its bitterness, which is why a splash of lemon juice is sometimes added.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Polyphenols in green tea help neutralize free radicals, supporting cellular health.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine and catechins may modestly boost metabolic rate and aid fat oxidation.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: A modest caffeine dose enhances alertness and cognitive performance.

items.title: Sugar‑free hydration
items.content: Provides fluid without added calories, making it ideal for hot weather.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular moderate consumption of green tea is linked to better lipid profiles and reduced heart disease risk.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience jitteriness, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine and polyphenols can affect the action of certain medications, such as blood thinners.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Green tea has mild acidity, which may irritate the stomach of individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the iced green tea chilled; optionally add a lemon wedge or a sprig of mint for extra aroma. It pairs well with light snacks, salads, and seafood dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle refrigerated at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Protect from prolonged exposure to direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna salad with cheese is a dish where tender tuna is mixed with creamy processed cheese, mayonnaise and spices. It is popular as a quick snack, sandwich filling, and salad topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Cream cheese gives the salad a smooth texture and helps protein absorption.
The salad is often served in school cafeterias and as sports nutrition.
Traditional recipes frequently include finely chopped onion and fresh herbs.
Canned tuna retains most of its nutrients even after long storage.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 supports heart health and reduces inflammation.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Tuna provides a complete set of amino acids needed for muscle repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, B6 and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese adds calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Fish or dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to fish or dairy proteins may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains high salt levels; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Mercury risk
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Cheese calories
items.content: Cream cheese adds calories and saturated fat, so portion size should be controlled.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the opened jar. Use it as a spread on bread, a filling for wraps, mix into vegetable salads, or enjoy it as a standalone snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened jar in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey bacon is a lean product made from turkey meat that has been smoked and pre‑cooked. The reduced‑sodium version contains roughly half the salt of regular bacon, making it a better choice for low‑sodium diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey bacon has about 30 % less fat than traditional pork bacon.
Sodium reduction is achieved through special salt blends and fermentation.
The product is ready to eat after a quick heat‑up – it can be added to salads, sandwiches, or microwaved.
Often used in athletes’ and health‑conscious diets because of its lower calorie and fat content.
Unlike many smoked meats, turkey bacon does not require additional pan‑frying.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using turkey instead of pork reduces saturated fat, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Less salt helps control blood pressure and reduces kidney strain.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A serving provides about 12 g of protein, aiding muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lower calories
items.content: Compared with regular bacon, calorie count is roughly 20 % lower.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: Like most smoked products, it may contain small amounts of nitrates, which should be limited with frequent consumption.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Certain brands may include flavorings or preservatives that can trigger sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey bacon is ready after reheating. Add it to omelets, salads, pasta, sandwiches, or serve alongside eggs. For a crispier texture, heat in a skillet for 1–2 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging. Once opened, consume within 5 days. When frozen, quality is maintained for up to 2 months.
